utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. This afternoon we'll continue the proceedings in this case. And before that, are there any other matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I guess this could come under the housekeeping matter category. From the last witness, which was Witness 119 [sic], we heard him state under oath that during the proofing session at one point the Prosecutor slammed a drawer and began accusing the gentleman of various things, including trying to protect Mr. Blagojevic. The Prosecutor neither affirmed nor denied that that conduct occurred. If -- and I believe we do need a clear record on this matter. If there is a denial, obviously, then the witness was either misspeaking or was making things up, which goes then to the witness's credibility. If there is an affirmation, however, then I believe at the very minimum there should be some kind of cautionary note to the Prosecution to cease and desist from such conduct during proofing sessions. I think that if a Defence lawyer had engaged in this sort of conduct, that Defence lawyer would be escorted out of this building, their badge taken away, thrown off the case, even before any due process. And I speak because -- I say this because in another case another Defence counsel for less conduct than what 119 [sic] witness stated was taken off the case and thrown out of the building before even having any due process accorded to her. Now, I think it is important to recognise that some witnesses when they're being proofed, may come under a certain amount of pressure, which may have an unfortunate and unintended, but nonetheless unfortunate result of causing the witness to be less than candid under oath here. I think we all get frustrated with witnesses. I know I do when I'm cross-examining someone and I know the Trial Chamber has cautioned me, and rightly so, on numerous occasions when I have been less than courteous to witnesses here in this courtroom. I think that should also apply during proofing sessions because I don't think that we want any witnesses to come here and to feel under duress or to be misspeaking the facts simply because they feel that while they're a witness today, tomorrow they may be a suspect and facing charges down the road. So at this point in time, Your Honour, I would like the Court to require from the Prosecution whether, in fact, this conduct occurred as 119 [sic], witness 119 [sic] has indicated. Because I think we do need a record. And as I indicated if there is a denial, I certainly would like to point that out in the record that this is directly going against the credibility of the Prosecution witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I wonder whether Mr. McCloskey would like to make a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is one of many allegations of misconduct that's been thrown at the Prosecution by both sides in this case. It's been my practice to not respond to this kind of allegation. But in this particular situation, I will. The witness that testified embellished quite a bit regarding that particular subject. He started with it when he was inflamed by Mr. Karnavas, and he started making false allegations against Dean Manning, several regarding the interview that never occurred. Then he went into the allegations against me. Now, I never screamed at the man. I did shut my drawer more loudly than I should have, and at the same time I did tell him that he shouldn't cover for Blagojevic, that he should just tell the truth. He was treated with respect and courtesy for the several hours that I spoke to him, as he indicated on the witness stand. There was no screaming and no abuse and no attempt to have him say anything but the truth. Now, I don't really have anything more to say on this subject. It is not -- I think the Judges -- you know me after all these many months. The record of the interviews both in court and the interviews that I was involved in in the investigation are before you and before the Defence. I am proud of the job I do; I am proud of the job I've done. I know it's a common tactic to put the Prosecution on trial. I don't think I really need to get down at that level and respond to this material every time it comes up. But if the Court wishes to have any further information or any other -- wants to ask me any questions, I stand here ready to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that at the end of the testimony of that witness, especially during the re-direct from the Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey particularly asked some questions to that witness. The record is there, and today Mr. McCloskey also made some explanations on the situation during the proofing session. So I think the matter is quite clear, and the objections from Mr. Karnavas has already been registered in the transcript. As for the weight that the Bench will attach to the testimony of that witness is a matter we have to deal with at a later stage. But anyway, I hope all the parties, no matter from the Prosecution or the Defence counsel, should pay due respect to the witness. It is a difficult time, I must confess, for a witness to be in the International Tribunal to give testimony. There will be some psychological impact to them, and this Bench would like to show great sympathy to the situation the witnesses are. So I hope in the future, no matter if the witness is the Prosecution's witness or the Defence's witness, they should do everything according to the Rules and pay due respect to the witness. I believe this is a warning, not only to the Prosecution but also to the Defence, because the Defence case will soon be coming at the beginning of next year. Thank you. So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, your witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, could you take a look at this piece of paper the usher has. Don't read it, but could you tell us, is that your name written on that paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go into private session briefly, Your Honour. Just a question or two on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, what kind of a facility did you work from the Dekic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: We were working in a family house. That was on two floors. We were staying up on the first floor with our equipment and the antennas were placed outside on the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you describe what your unit and what yourself were doing at the time before and after the fall of the enclave in this house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: That centre in that house was a place from where we were surveying the radio communications. Mostly the communications of the police forces; the Republika Srpska MUP or the public security -- the centre for security of Zvornik; the special units, the wolves of the Drina; as well as the frontlines of the 1st Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you roughly describe again by pointing to the map the area that you were able to listen to with your equipment from this house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: The Dekici centre was able to cover the area of Kozluk, Petkovci, Zvornik, all the way to Cerska, perhaps. And from Gradina, we were able to monitor the combat activities in Srebrenica as well as everything that was going on around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you describe in particular detail how you and your workers were able to monitor the other side? How did the -- what was the actual process by which you received this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Since the 24th Division was not as well equipped with electronic equipment as some other units, we then had to adjust to the situation and to do what we could. The work procedures were as follows: One of the operators would be scanning on certain equipment, specifically the ECR-100 equipment. When a certain frequency was found, the frequency would be handed over to another place to a piece of equipment that was always on and that was always covering that frequency. Each conversation that took place, especially a more important conversation, would be written down by the operator on a piece of paper, and this would be conveyed to me. Although, most of the time I was also present, so I was also able to hear everything. It was my task to pass that on up to our superiors. I did that by using an induction telephone, using military telephone communications. At the end of the day, when the combat activities had been completed, most of those pieces of paper were copied into a notebook, a logbook. And because I was there and because I was -- as well as the superior command both had all the information or the data available to us, some of those pieces of paper were destroyed. So it is very likely that a large majority of that information did not end up in those notebooks and logbooks. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me take you back to the point where the operator is, as you've described, writing the information down on a piece of paper. What is he actually listening to when he's writing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Well, he's listening in to the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is he listening to the conversation live as it happens, or is he listening to a recorded version that had been recorded by him or others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: He's listening in to live conversations as they are going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After -- in the period after the fall of Srebrenica or just before, did you have the capacity or the ability to tape conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, using a standard castaphone [phoen] cassette recorder, but at that time we did not do that because that would be too slow and would not at that particular time represent any asset for us. It would just be time-consuming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe how the operators were able to write-down the information they were hearing at the same time it was coming over the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: The persons whom I've listed, the operators, in other words, did this work throughout the war, and they were able to write quite fast. So that this posed no problem at all for them to write these things down, in fact they also used a number of abbreviations. For instance, as an example, if they were checking communications -- communication check, they would not write-down in extensive communication check, just p/v which meant communication check and similar. So there were such examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you find the information that you were identifying and recording in this manner to be reliable?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object. It calls for speculation. He's asking the gentleman whether he found it to be reliable. There's no recording of the information, and how could the gentleman check for reliability. If they want to establish, I think more foundation needs to be laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: First of all, I think the Prosecution just asked a very general question concerning with a particular piece of the intercepts. I believe if there is a need, the Prosecution will ask more questions on that area. Secondly, this person, as we were told, is in charge of this matter. And I believe that he could tell us what is his evaluation and judgement of those intercepts. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you find the material you were receiving and intercepting and documenting, as you've described, reliable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, we found it -- I found it reliable, 100 per cent reliable, because I was personally there in 99 per cent of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that information -- do you know if that information was used by the superiors that you have told us you provided it to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I suppose they did, because at that time we were the only source of information from the territory which was under the control of the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the site at Okresanica and Konjuh, of the Bosnian Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how was the work you were doing different from the work they were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Well, we did reconnaissance of communications at a tactical level, which is to say that we were quite limited equipment-wise, whereas Okresanica and Konjuh had, by far, more sophisticated equipment so that they had operation and strategic communication lines. Namely, communications which took place by phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to show you a couple of things, and I first want to show you what has been marked as, I believe, P121/B. There should be a -- it's a photocopied version, but I want to give you just what is not a photocopy. And it's got some red marks in it just to assist you in perhaps finding some things. Now, can you tell us what this book is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: This is one of these logbooks that I referred to before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And is that for the time period in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us about this book, where it was during the time period that it was used by your unit and how it ended up here in The Hague, as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: This book was held at the centre. After that, it was handed over to me and was at the command of the division in Zivinice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "it was at the centre," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It was actually at the interception station where it was being kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Dekici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when it was handed over to you, where did you keep it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I kept it in my safe at the division command in Zivinice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at some point did you provide that to anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: We were given an order to surrender any such materials to the Prosecutor. So I handed over this notebook with some other items.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we might as well, since you've mentioned it, go to those other items. And again I'll show you the original packet of material, which should be 122 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Going back to P121, there has been an improper foundation laid because Mr. McCloskey has not asked him when he turned these over. When he says they were at the centre, how they were stored, how they were kept, whose custody they were in. There's been no proof of chain of custody of this document P121, and I hope that he'll prove the same for 122. We don't know when these documents were turned over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this is a subject for your cross-examination, Ms. Sinatra, but now we are dealing with the 122. Maybe in this piece of document, Mr. McCloskey could lay more foundations for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, since he had discussed this I thought we would save time doing them both together, since as he's mentioned they were both provided together at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could you look at this exhibit, this stack of papers, which is 122. Was that turned over to the Prosecutor, along with the notebook that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this stack of papers represents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: These are reports which came in to me from the Gradina centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, what do you mean when you say "reports"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: These were collected data, all data, which were obtained at the Gradina centre, which data was then submitted by way of reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "data," what kind of data in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: This was data which was collected by electronic reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that data from the enemy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Is that -- do you know how the information came to be written on those pieces of paper? You've talked to us about pieces of paper before, how were those pieces in paper in front of you different or related to the pieces of paper that an operator writes down at the same time he's listening to an intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It was the same system as the one applied at Dekici. That was that we used a piece of paper, and you can see in the exhibit there are many abbreviations used, which would then be later analysed and put together in the form of reports. Then afterwards, through the 243rd Brigade, which was located at Kladanj, this data was then submitted to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have described the pieces of paper, and that exhibit as reports. Are there any in that binder -- excuse me, in that little packet of papers, are there any of the original pieces of paper that were used to dictate the actual intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Most of that material is -- are those reports or are they the actual piece of paper that the intercept was written on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Most of these are actually the original pieces of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Because the report has a certain form, has a certain stamp of the brigade, the protocol, whereas from this we can conclude because it is in manuscript and because of the abbreviations that are used, which I referred to earlier. It is obvious this is written in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us when you first became in possession of those piles of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Specifically this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: That was during a visit to the Gradina centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what time frame, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It may have been August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do with this stack of paper when you got it from Gradina in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I took it to the command of the division, and I left it there with the rest of the filing material of the files in the safe box.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when was the next time you saw the material, the piles of paper I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It was in my strongbox all the time, until the time when I handed it over to the team of investigators, together with this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the person you handed the material over with, both the notebook you've been referring to and this exhibit, Exhibits 121 and 122?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I believe it was Stephania -- Stephanie, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there any other material related to tactical intercepts that you were able to find and turn over to the Office of the Prosecutor than these two exhibits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I -- I didn't hand anything, except these two things to the Prosecution, anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you look for other records of tactical intercepts for that time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I did, but the bulk of it had been handed over to the filed in the archives of the 2nd Corps. And the rest of it was accidentally, as it were, because I had a number of problems when I was handing over the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? What problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Many people told me, these are just ordinary scraps of paper, it is worth nothing. It was mostly because of such reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what did you do with these two exhibits when those problems arose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Well, I returned them into the strongbox and I kept them there until I handed them over to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know if there was a notebook for Gradina like there was for Dekic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No, no. Because reports from Gradina would be submitted in different form. In Dekici, I was personally in Dekici so that there was no need for reports of the kind sent from Gradina to be submitted from Dekici. Because we would be losing too much time, wasting too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to try and clarify, the pieces of paper from Dekici, those that you called reports, are those reports of the intercepts or are they actual handwritten notes that were taken at the time that you were listening to them? I'm talking about the ones from Gradina, not Dekici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: As for Gradina, we have the original conversations which were written down as they were being conducted -- or listened in to. And then we have reports which would come on several occasions. It was not just a single form report -- actually, it all depended on how urgent the information was. So at the end of the day, such a report would be, again, submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you to just take a look in particular in the book from Dekici. Were you asked by the OTP, by Ms. Stephanie, just to look for any particular kind of substantive material in those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What were you asked to look for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I was asked to submit if there was anything associated with the period of the fall of Srebrenica and after the fall of Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could go to the -- in the book where it's dated 14 July. It's page 7 of the English translation, and in your book it should be our little addition, our ERN number 8952. And do you find a reference in there on page 7 at the top of the page, and it says: "For Maric, Miladinovic, Mitrovic, engineers to come at Nedjo's end with the excavator in order to widen the road." Do you see that reference? He said "vidim" and maybe he should turn on his --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I should know what "vidim" means by now, but I don't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you -- let me ask you again. Did you -- do you see that little reference that I spoke of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And is that one of the references you pointed out to Ms. Stephanie?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I am going to have to object at the moment to the witness testifying to the contents of this. He did say he was the commander at Dekici, but he also said that these little pieces of paper were written down by other people. Unless the Prosecutor can say he did write this down and this is his handwriting and he remembers receiving this conversation, I don't believe that he can properly authenticate this handwriting or the contents of this notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think we have come that far as to the contents of the intercepts yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But we'll see how this will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: My understanding is what he's reading out of the notebook at the moment is what he considers handwritten notes from an intercept dealing with the engineering department and mentioning the name Miladinovic, which if he has personal knowledge of this intercept, if that is his handwriting, because I believe he is testifying to intercepted conversations at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe you have to allow the Prosecution to ask some questions of who put those words down and who is the writer for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're getting there, I hope. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe Mr. McCloskey is putting the horse before the cart in that he's having him testify from the contents before he's laying the proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you identified this for Ms. Frease, did you have any memory of this actual intercept?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. Mr. McCloskey is testifying. The witness has only referred to Ms. Stephanie through his testimony now. Mr. McCloskey has added Frease. Now if the witness tells us it's Stephanie Frease, we will -- would like the evidence to come from the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, do it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: She's correct. I accidentally threw the last name in. I don't think he knows that last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you pointed this out for Ms. Frease, did you have any recollection of this particular -- Ms. Stephanie, sorry, I don't know her as Ms. Stephanie, so that's my problem, Ms. Stephanie --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to try one more time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you identified this for Ms. Stephanie, did you recollect this at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you explain that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: At the time when this conversation was being conducted, I was at the centre myself. So I could hear the conversation being conducted, and we commented on it, associated with this particular expression, the excavating of the road, penetrating of the road. It was inconceivable for us that at such a time of war somebody was going to work on the road. And this is what I emphasised in my report, which I sent to the command of the division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as for the handwriting in the book, do you know whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And whose handwriting do you think that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go into private session, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know is any of the handwriting in that notebook from anyone besides the people who were working for you during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No, I -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about if we go back to Exhibit 121 for a second, the handwriting in those reports and those transcripts, would those be from anyone -- would those be from the people who were working for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And those are the people you've already named?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any other questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could have a break now, and after the break there will be the cross-examination. And we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before coming to testify here, you met with the Prosecution, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe that was on 15 December. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And before meeting the Prosecutor on that day, you had met with the Office of the Prosecution on three prior occasions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The first time was I believe in 1999. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I can't remember exactly, but I think that that was it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May 17th, 1999. At that time, where did you meet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: At the Konjuh facility, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So they came to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during that meeting, that interview was not tape recorded, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And of course you have been able -- you were provided with a copy of the, well, I guess, summary of the interview, and it's approximately a page and a half. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me. Received when?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I have in my possession a page and a half of that interview that is dated May 17th, 1999. Were you provided with a copy of that summary of the interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Not at that occasion, but I did have the opportunity to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How long did you speak with the gentleman from the Office of the Prosecution that generated only this page and a half of a summary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I think this was a very long time ago, and I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, was it more than an hour or less than an hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Perhaps about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And during that time, did you provide them with any documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And on that occasion when you met with them, you were still in the army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you met with them for a second time on 18 October 2002. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from that, I again have what would appear to be approximately a one-page summary of the interview. Were you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, but not again on that same occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, where was that interview conducted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Well, we had a few of those conversations. I think one of them was at the corps command, but I cannot recall the exact date when it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say "a few," you mean there are other occasions that I haven't mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I think that there were some later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you met with them for the second time on 18 October 2002, you were no longer in the army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And maybe we can go into private session for this one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during this interview, did you provide them -- did you provide the gentleman from the Prosecution with any documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No. We just discussed those documents. I had promised that I would try to find a part of the documents or just to check whether any of them remained in the possession of anybody, just by chance. But I didn't actually find anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Just to make sure that I'm clear, from 1999, from May 17, 1999, to 18 October 2002, were there any meetings that we don't have information about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if you did not hand over any notebooks or any documents on 18 October 2002, can we conclude the documents were handed over during your first meeting back in May 17, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then again -- now, the second meeting, was that tape recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how long did that take, the interviewing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Again, I cannot remember. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, was it a long session or a short session? And maybe you can use the last meeting that you had here in The Hague as a reference for the length of time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It didn't take that long. Maybe -- once again, I think that it took about an hour at the most, as far as I can recall. But as I said before, it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then you met again on 29 October 2003. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about approximately two months ago, less than two months ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, this time it would appear, because it's reflected in the report, that you met in the Sarajevo field office of the Office of the Prosecution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Perhaps about two hours, maybe a little longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And was that meeting tape recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I don't know that either. I didn't record it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Was that the first time that you had been to that field office in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during that meeting, did you provide any further documents or any notebooks to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, as I understand your testimony, some -- the documents that you did provide to the Prosecution were not part of the archive.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No. They were kept as an archive, but they were actually never placed in the central archives of the corps command. So the majority of the documents that were stored we did not manage to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's stick with -- let's focus a little bit on the archiving or the keeping of these particular documents. According to your testimony, you made an effort to have them archived. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These are documents that you believe are 100 per cent reliable. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the people that you were trying to convince that these documents should be archived and kept for posterity, these were the people for whom you had worked for. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: These were people from the command of the division who were working on the archiving of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And these people were part of the Bosnian Muslim army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So they of all people would have an interest in making sure that reliable documents, especially documents which may have a historical importance, they were the ones that thought these documents were unworthy of being kept. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Those people didn't even look at the contents of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yet these were the same people, the same people, that were in charge of collecting documents, not just for historical purposes but also for the purpose of providing those documents to the Office of the Prosecution, as they have done so since approximately 1995, 1996. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes. They are those people, but again, I am repeating, they did not even look at them. They just looked at the protocol stamp and the -- they looked at the documents which did not have such a stamp by the filing or the protocol service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say "they." Who are they? Is it more than one person? Or was it just some clerk who was just dismissive of accepting these documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: They were members of the unit who were working. I think there were two of them who were working on the maintenance or upkeep of that archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And according to you, to your testimony, in your words, they said that they were "worth nothing." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Again, I say they didn't even look at the contents of the documents. They would just look to see if the document had a stamp or it didn't have one, and that was what they used as a criteria of the value of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My question was that as you put it in direct examination, in your own words, they told you that these documents were "worth nothing." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That they were just ordinary scraps of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the process that was used in the field in Dekici, as I understand your testimony, was not a process by which conversations were recorded on tape before transcribed on to paper. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Nothing was taped in Dekici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it wasn't taped because there were no -- there was no such equipment available. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many operators were working at any particular time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: At that time in Dekici, everybody was working. During the course of the day while the combat activities were going on, everybody was working. In the evening when the combat operations ceased, the people rested. And you can see in the logbooks that there were no shifts at that time. Everybody was working all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me rephrase my question a little bit. How many operators were there? In other words, how many were listening and writing down conversations at any particular moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Four, and I was the fifth person there. So there were about three or four of them. It depends. Sometimes one of them was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you had three or four devices working at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: There were perhaps more devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And so if there were more devices and as I understand there was a fairly large crew, then at any -- there were times when all devices were being used at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were the operators, did they have headsets, like we are wearing today, listening into the conversations? Or could the conversations be heard by everyone in the room at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: They had headsets which they would switch on occasionally, if perhaps several conversations took place at the same time. If several networks were not active at the same time, however, then the conversation could be audible to everyone in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. And you were the commander, correct, the komandir of this particular unit. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, there were times when you were just monitoring the situation, making sure that everybody was doing their work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if an operator is wearing headsets and if there is more than one operator at the time wearing headsets and you are there monitoring the situation of your staff, it's not possible, is it, for you to listen in on every conversation and to make sure that at that -- the conversation that is being listened to is being written out verbatim by each and every operator. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. If everybody's wearing headsets and if all the networks are working at the same time. But in the notes from the Dekici area, you can see that things were not written down verbatim. I am repeating once again, when one network was active at a given time, then all the operators and myself, if I was there, would be able to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was there a time when there was more than one being active, or as soon as you locked into a conversation, all the other operators would stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No. They wouldn't stop, because if a conversation appeared on another network and the operator who was sitting at that post would then switch to his headset and continue to monitor the situation so that he would not be disturbing the person -- the other person who was taking down a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you're not able to listen to these conversations because there's more than one going on, you cannot say here today, as you have done so on direct examination, that you found them to be - the recording of those conversations - you found them to be, in your own words, 100 per cent reliable. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I did say that, because I spent a lot of time with those people during the war and I know how experienced they are in their work. And I also said that because the majority of those conversations were not taken down verbatim, that somebody said this or that. But a conversation that was heard was conveyed in a summary fashion, and the people who actually did that had a lot of experience in this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if there were times where the operator was unclear of what had been said in the conversation that he was monitoring, there were no capability, were there, for the operator at some other point to rewind the tape and to replay the conversation to make sure that there would be a 100 per cent accurate record. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: We were not able to do that, because we didn't have the technical means to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what if I were to tell you that other operators, intercept operators, have come here and testified and have indicated that at times they would need to replay, rewind and replay, the tape recorded conversation many, many times in order to make sure that they understood what, in fact, was being said. So my question is: How is it that they, who seem to be equally as qualified as your men, needed to do that, while your men did not require to have a tape-recording in order to make sure that what was being written out was true, accurate, and complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of the evidence as it's come in. The witness clearly said this -- many times this was a summary and not a complete verbatim transcript, which is what we know the other people strove for. With that kind of misstatement of the evidence, that becomes argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But from the question, although I don't like it, it takes about eight lines, but I think it's a reasonable question. The Defence counsel is entitled to ask this question. The problem is that this question is too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll -- I can rephrase, Your Honour, if that's necessary for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's see whether the witness understands your question or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I do understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Actually, these conversations took place by phone, by radio relay communication line. This is a kind of continued, uninterrupted conversation. It is very hard to take down verbatim and put it down on paper. And at the time they wanted us to relay to them conversation recordings that were 100 per cent identical to the actual conversations that had taken place. So that was a totally different type of conversation to the one that we did. The first were the radio relay conversations that I talked about and the other ones were telephone communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I don't see anything --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Radio communications are much easier to monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there's nothing that we can -- that you can produce to us, such as a tape-recording, that would give us -- that we could listen to to compare what was on the notebooks and what was actually heard. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we don't have those scraps of paper that were used to write down these conversations, albeit in shorthand with abbreviations, which were later written into the notebooks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No. Not from the Dekici facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because those scraps of paper were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: They were destroyed at the time, during the time we worked there, because the data was immediately accessible to me, i.e., to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, at the other location, in Gradina, were those conversations being tape recorded before being transcribed into the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it the same procedure was used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes. The same procedure and you have the notes in the papers, in the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you were not there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were not the commander there of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: This was just one squad of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if I understand you correctly, they were your men at that location, but you were not there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in that location, I take it, was that -- were they responsible for monitoring the area around the Bratunac Brigade or around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when Srebrenica was falling and after it fell, am I correct in understanding that you were not in Gradina at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, you are. I wasn't there. I was at Dekici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while you are able to tell us with an incredible degree of certainty as to the reliability of the work product coming from Dekici, that is 100 per cent, because you were present and you were able to observe, I take it you cannot be as reliable for Gradina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes. As regards control, I cannot. I cannot say that I was there, because I wasn't there. But these are also tested people, experienced people, who had done such work for a long time. And if certain things are compared analytically, those reports, and our reports, we can see that there is a high level of coincidence, meaning that they were done properly. I couldn't be at two places at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that, but I was just using your test where you said that in Dekici you could be 100 per cent sure that it was reliable because you were there 99 per cent of the time. That was one of the bases of your certainty. And if we use that as a test for Gradina, then it would follow that you could not be as certain. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, not as certain as in the Dekici case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it as in Dekici, we do not have those scraps of paper for all of the intercepts or all of the conversations that were written down. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No, you don't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did they use a notebook there or was it reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: In Dekici you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, in Gradina. I'm sorry. In Gradina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: From Gradina reports would be submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So I take it the recordkeeping method for Gradina was even less stringent as it was for Dekici, because one you have notebooks, the other one you just have some reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: This all lasted until the organisation of our work. Reports had to be submitted from Gradina, because I wasn't there and I had no telephone communication with them. So that reports had to be submitted in that form through the protected radio communication line. And while I was in Dekici, I had at my disposal a telephone communication line so that there was no need for any such practices. It would be only a mental waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when Srebrenica was falling, were you getting reports from Gradina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you sending your reports on to Sarajevo or Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, I was, to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it Tuzla was being kept notified as the situation was progressing on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness P119.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I want to just follow up on some questions that counsel for Mr. Blagojevic has just asked, especially regarding the reliability of the Dekici notes that you have in your notebook. Let me ask you, first you said that you scanned the frequencies with your ICR-100s. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, we had that particular piece of equipment and another two -- one or two items of equipment which could scan various frequency bands.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I do want to go back. You said that you went to secondary school in electronics. That's the equivalent of like a high school most everywhere else, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you were not a ham radio operator, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Not at school -- yes, when I was in the military, I was a ham radio operator at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: When you say "ham radio operator," did you achieve the international licensing that goes along with being a licensed ham radio operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Now I have. Now I have. At that particular time, I only had become a member of one of the ham radio operator's clubs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: We're talking about 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It was war in 1995 so that I didn't -- I had had a lot of experience at that time with radio engineering and repair and maintenance of radio equipment and the operation of same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But you weren't licensed as a ham radio operator in 1995, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No, I wasn't licensed as a ham radio operator.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: After you scanned the channels with your ECR-100, then you have to lock into a frequency, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, practically that's the way it works.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And then you said your operators would write down some notes on a piece of paper. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: After scanning and locking in with the frequency, you connected with another piece of equipment. And then we take notes on scraps of paper in the way I already described.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you did state that these scraps of paper and the notes were often taken in shorthand. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and I also explained what particular form of shorthand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Shorthand to you is just a set of abbreviations that y'all use, or is it really the actual shorthand that stenographers use?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I do not know what stenographers use, but I could give you a couple of examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Is it an art that you study shorthand in school where you learn to write shorthand, or is it something that was made up by your communications division?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: This is an experience from the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Once they're written on a piece of paper, then they're -- all these little notes are passed to you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes. I could immediately hear the bulk of the information immediately myself. There was no need [Realtime transcript read in error "only"] for it to be passed on to me, but when I couldn't hear it personally, when it was being listened in by somebody else who was wearing headsets, then the radio operators could convey such information to me with such scraps of paper on such paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And then if you determined that the scraps of paper had some information that was important, then you would get on the hard telephone line and you would pass it to superiors. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And is the induction telephone, the military telephone you're talking about, that's a hard line or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So what basically happens is you go through these little pieces of paper, and then you hand these back to the people whose handwriting you recommend. And at the end of the day part of them are recorded in a logbook and part of them are not. Is that what happens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It all depended on the time. It all depended on the time available for us to note all this down in various notebooks and logbooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: At the end of the day, isn't it true that it would be very difficult to decipher shorthand pieces of paper from conversations that were happening all at one time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: These were not abbreviations that were not understandable. These are normally used abbreviations in radio communications which normally use secret codes or secret designations. And once used, it is not repeated again. I will give you an example. What you have in the exhibit, for instance you have see Lovac, Lovac 1, L-o-v-a-c. So you just write that once, and if you don't manage to write that again the next time you come across that you only write "L" or "L1" so whoever is deciphering or reading it knows this refers to the entire word, Lovac. And the other example which I gave was the checking of the communication, it is p/v. It is not the whole word komandir, but just K/O, and so on and so forth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Sinatra, to interrupt you. I have a problem with the transcript and I want to know if I heard it correctly. But in page 40, line 12, it says now: It was only for it to be passed, something like that, on to me. And I heard the witness say -- or at least the translation: "It was not necessary." May I ask which is the correct thing, because afterwards we wouldn't understand this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I don't have that on my screen, but I'm going to assume that it had to do with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: It's already passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, it's passed for me. Your Honour, if you would like to clarify this for me, I would be very happy since because I can't see it. If you would like to ask the witness a question at this point I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Sorry to interrupt you, sir, I have a clarification to ask from you. When you were describing this process on the taking the notes down and then passing on your pieces of paper to you, you said that you were there. So was it necessary to give you these pieces of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In replying to one of these questions, I remarked that these conversations were not important on paper at the time when I was there. They were important for me if I wasn't there or if the conversation was being listened in to by people with headphones and if I was not in the room. So in such cases, I would be given such conversation on paper, and then I would try to analyse the content and then send it on to the command. Any other conversations which I could hear myself was not needed for -- I didn't need it on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: This was my understanding. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: In fact, the papers were destroyed they were so unimportant to you at the time. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: At that time they were unimportant. Well, had I known that the situation would evolve in this way, they would have probably been preserved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Let me ask you, you're from the Zvornik area. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you know that all the area around Zvornik is highly mountainous. It's in a valley, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And from Dekici where you were monitoring, you know that all communications from Zvornik had to go through a communications post that they had in Karakaj above their command headquarters. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: These were radio relay communications and radio relay communications have no limitations. There exists certain relay repeaters so that the configuration of the terrain is of no particular bearing on the operation of such links. Secondly, we chose Dekici because it was a location that had been tested before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Now, maybe I misunderstood, but I understood that radio waves travel in a line of sight format, in a straight line. And in order for radio communications to get to Zvornik, they had to either have a relay station that was close by or they had to be sent to another relay station, which was about 50 kilometres away from Zvornik. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: A radio relay connection to which you listen to before is directed, and for that kind of connection, the centres and the elevations are very important, while the radio connections disperse equally in all directions. So this doesn't play a major part, but the configuration of the terrain plays a much greater role in the second case. I can clarify it even more for you if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You agree with me, then, that the configuration of the countryside does affect, one way or the other, the reception of radio communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, it does, because if it didn't matter, we wouldn't have to be in Dekici, we could also be in Zivinice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And from Dekici when you're receiving radio communications from the relay station that's about 50 kilometres away, you can't tell where that communication originated, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: In radio communications, when there are -- in many conversations, locations are also mentioned, and you have them in your exhibits as well. And if one participant mentions it and says, I am -- I'm just giving an example, I'm at Crni Vrh, we know where this Crni Vrh is. So the participants were the ones who would reveal their locations to us. But in radio communications, it's very difficult to know the location of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In fact, in radio communications, if you were just picking up a relay from the relay station, you couldn't tell whether it was from Vlasenica or Zvornik or Bratunac, could you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: We knew by the frequencies. We knew by that who the participants were, but you have mentioned the frequency 164.50 megahertz, this frequency is mentioned there -- 050, that frequency belongs to the Zvornik police. We knew that. The public security centre of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you did say one of the main targets of your communications was the MUP in Zvornik. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, one of the targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the other target that you were set to monitor was the Drina Wolves. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the other target you were set to monitor was the frontline of the Zvornik Brigade, which would have been at Snagovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Generally, yes, we were monitoring the radio communications of the Zvornik Brigade, the frontline as well as the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: When you say "the units," you could not target into the radio receptions of Standard headquarters, could you, because it had to go through a relay centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: We were able to hear that. I am again talking about the radio relay connections. We were able to hear them, because if one of the participants who was perhaps close to us, they also were not able to hear the Standard command. There was something that is called a communications centre of that brigade, which would be located at a dominant elevation. And all of those who could not hear themselves amongst each other would be linked through that centre. He would -- they would pick it up and then convey it further.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to skip over some of my notes to go to that. That communications centre up above the Zvornik Brigade headquarters in Karakaj, it had a secret code name, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Do you mean their radio centre?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Their radio centre was known as Lovac, wasn't it, because you mentioned that name earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No. Lovac, Lovac appeared during the combat activities around Srebrenica, but Premijer was actually quite active and that also had the role of a centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Let me ask you. You know Lovac 1, that's a secret code name for Dragan Obrenovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I know that and I think that's what it says in the documents as well, he was some sort of chief of staff of something.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the conversation you're talking about is between Lovac 1 and Lovac, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And Lovac 1 is asking Lovac to contact someone up at Snagovo to release a couple of engineers that you've mentioned. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is correct, but I cannot remember it now exactly. But I think it is something to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And Lovac 1 at that time was not at the brigade headquarters, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No, he wasn't, probably not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And Lovac was someone named Brano Mikic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I don't know that. I cannot say that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But Lovac was not at Standard or the Zvornik Brigade headquarters either, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly, and I'm saying again in radio communications it's very hard to know the exact locations of the participants. And what is known is most often known if somebody reveals it in the course of their conversation, as opposed to radio relay communications where you know the end speakers for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And Lovac is the one who called Milan Maric, the commander up at Snagovo, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I cannot remember, perhaps if you can show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, is Lovac the one who called up to Snagovo and asked for the release of the two engineers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Perhaps I can look at that conversation to see what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I don't have P121. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the Prosecution would like to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. He has -- we can provide him with the book. It's probably the easiest to look at, and if he can go to 14 July, where I think I -- he had pointed us out earlier, he should be able to find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I don't know if I might be provided an English copy of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we've -- that's been done, but I -- you can have mine if we -- actually, we should have another -- let me just give you mine because I've marked it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, would you please thank Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I believe that what P121 says is a conversation between Lovac 1, who we know is Obrenovic, and Lovac. And it says: "Are you in communication with Maric?" Now, you know that Milan Maric was the commander up at Snagovo. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I am not aware of that fact, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, your conversation is between Lovac 1 and Lovac, and it appears that Obrenovic is asking for Maric, Miladinovic, and Mitrovic, to come to Nedjo's end with two excavators in order to widen the road. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: We cannot establish that either, because as you can see Lovac and Lovac 1: "Are you in communication with Maric?" And then after that they went to a different frequency. I don't know whether that was translated. To -- that's channel 274, Sava 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So you don't know if this was all one conversation or if they were doing what we call frequency hopping at the moment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It's the same conversation, but it was carried out on two frequencies. It began on one and completed -- finished on another.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But are you saying that you followed this conversation from one frequency to the next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Then if that's true, it looks like Dragan Obrenovic is asking for Maric, Miladinovic, and Mitrovic, to come to Nedjo's end. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I cannot say who, but this is a conversation between Lovac and Lovac 1, between Obrenovic and Lovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you know all the other secret codes, but you don't know who Lovac is. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Well, we don't know all the other ones either, because at the time and in that work generally, data and locations are more important to us, where the participant is located. His name is not important to us, only the location and the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And that's true of all of your communications, isn't it? When you intercept these communications, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: During the combat activities around Srebrenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I just want to go back to July 14th, just to remind the Trial Chamber, that was the day of heaviest radio traffic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Because the Muslims from Srebrenica and the 28th Division, the Muslim column, were fleeing from the Srebrenica area toward the Zvornik area. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Towards the liberated or the free territory of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: They were headed right towards Zvornik, and Zvornik was in jeopardy of falling to the Muslim column at that point, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I don't think that they were going towards Zvornik. They were going through the woods, and I believe that many of them didn't even know where they were going, because the town had already been taken. So they were mostly moving through the woods. We also had cases of people coming out after 20 or 30 days, out of the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I want to go back to some general questions about your expertise, since you were commander of this tactical intercept unit. The difference between a regular communications system and a tactical intercept company or squad is that you're actually on the front possibly in danger of being attacked at that moment also, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, in principle that is so. Near the frontlines, near the lines where the combat activity is taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I want to ask you if you're familiar with your expertise with something called Operativno Maskiranje. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, I think I know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
