utterances.text: And it's another word for operational masking or misinformation or decoying or planting fake conversations or providing the enemy with false data, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: This was perhaps tried in this conversation relating to the widening of the road. That is why that conversation was suspicious to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, also part of masking is using false names, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but I think that none of my men would use my name as a false piece of information for the purpose of masking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, but you were in the anti-electronic warfare unit. Other people and other code names were changed interchangeably, weren't they, during war times and combat times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were changed and some remained the same throughout the whole war. Are you thinking about the secret names, the code names?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the code names, and that channel switching that you referred to in P121, it was a common part of masking, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes, if you don't know which channel it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Now, you did testify earlier that there were more documents from your facility having to do with July 14th, 15th, and 16th, 1995, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: There were a lot of notes from this facility. I even remember some of them, but unfortunately they're not here with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And a lot of the documents you sent in to what we would call a black hole. You sent them off to the archive of the 2nd Corps, and you've never seen them again. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, I'm just trying to wrap this up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Now, you were originally in the 24th Division, but you became a part of the 28th Division. That was the division fleeing from Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I was a member of the 24th Division. On arrival of a part of the people from the 28th Division, which -- then a new division was formed. It was the new 28th Division. So I was a member of that division later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Was that in July of 1995, though. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No. This didn't happen in July. It happened a little bit later. I cannot remember the date, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Going back to P121 also, I just want to make sure that what your communications represents is Lovac 1 calling Lovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: In the first part of the conversation, yes, it is. I'm not sure in the rest of the message who it is, because usually when they would switch to a new frequency in -- as in this specific case, secret or code names are not mentioned anymore. They just continue with the conversation or they would just say: Are you there? The answer would be yes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But you're pretty sure that the second part of this conversation was a continuation of the one you've notated as Lovac 1 to Lovac. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Quite sure, since we knew the frequency that they switched to. So we would just move from one piece of equipment to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: When an operator makes a note in the book that it was premodulated, does that mean that the voice of the person speaking was altered or changed in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Premodulation can occur for technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But it means the voice is not one that you would normally hear, it sounds different, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: A little bit different.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we might take a break, I can wrap this up in 10, 15 minutes when we come back, if you would let me just have one moment with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, and we'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to ask right now if the Prosecution has no objection, but we only have one piece of live evidence that is an -- a recording of conversations, intercepted conversations. That came from the Krstic trial. And I have a CD of it. I have asked the audio both to be prepared, and I just wanted to play a few moments of it and question the witness as to whether these are normal -- normally -- normal operations for the reception of interceptions. This is what it sounds like. Because we have no other record and the Prosecutor, Mr. McCloskey, said he has no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends on whether this piece of the record is relevant to this witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not relevant as far as content goes, but it is relevant as far as whether this is what it sounds like when you're intercepting conversations. And I think it's very important for the Trial Chamber to understand what it sounds like when they hear all these conversations going on at one time and they're trying to pick and choose and transcribe and, of course, this facility did not record. But this is the only one we have that is similar to it and this is the last intercept witness. I ask the Court's indulgence for one and a half minutes of an example of what it sounds like. It's been marked as D61/3. They're ready to prompt it up if we might just listen to it for one and a half minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So there's no objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. This -- for one and a half minutes, it's a tape that is not from his unit, but it's maybe roughly similar to the kind of thing. And he will be able to probably tell us a bit about it. I know you're now practically experts in this field. No -- I think you know what this means, so it's not going to be -- shouldn't be prejudicial in any way for either side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we've just heard an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to ask you any questions from the content of these conversations, but you have five of these going at one time in your -- at Dekici, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: This is not at all that kind of conversation. And I repeat, although I have already said, this is a conversation conducted by radio relay communication. It is the same as if it were conducted between two telephone parties, whereas the conversations that we monitored were conducted perhaps like the security arrangements that you have here, I mean the stations and the devices of the security here. As I have said before, this kind of conversation is impossible to take down verbatim. That is why at Konjuh, it was possible at Konjuh and Okresanica where they had the necessary equipment for taping and recording and putting it into their computers. Whereas, the conversations that we had were of a different nature. This was a continued conversation which never ceases. In our conversations, the ones that we were taping, that we were taking down, rather, we had on occasion a lapse of half a minute from one side to another, so that one had ample time to put it down. It depended on the hearing capacity of the actual participant. So it was transmitted and retransmitted and could be confirmed during this lapse of time. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, as a technical -- tactical intercept operator, actually the tactical radio intercepts were less clear than these were, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: They could be less clear, just as they were -- if they were not clear to us, they were not clear to the other participant, so that often repetitions were demanded. I think this happened more in the case of Gradina, that they had such repetitions of the one and the same thing for several times, because that meant the participant could not hear properly and was asking for a repetition in order to relay it to someone who was on an elevation. But technically speaking, it could happen that conversations were unintelligible. Of course, if there were only two participants, it could remain unintelligible and unclear, but we could manage, if there were more than two, that is, and if we could manage to have it cleared up. And in radio communications, we have unidirectional communication in contrast to this particular link. You can never have two parties speaking simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You had several conversations going at one time from your different receivers, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: We were monitoring a number of frequencies at the same time, so there were a number of conversations being monitored at the same time. And each, as I have already said, each of the operators had their own headgear on and were each taking down their own conversation that they were following. But it was hardly likely that they could miss anything, because this is the kind of communication, the kind of traffic that we had. You can see in the evidence we also mentioned some telegrams, some cables, some numbers, which are being read like in a telephone conversation, but still they managed to write them down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, also I would like to remind you and for you to remind the Trial Chamber, this tape was the first week in August. On July 14th, the radio traffic was much heavier than it was the first week in August, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: As far as radio communications were concerned, yes. In a single radio network -- in a single radio network, only one participant can talk. So on one frequency at that moment you can only hear one participant. If another one should happen to appear, it is unintelligible to us as well as to the party to whom that particular message is being addressed. That means that as far as that was concerned, it did not really pose a great problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, you do admit that there was much heavier radio traffic, though, on the 14th of July than there was the first week in August. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you are aware that Dragan Obrenovic had another secret code name, Avala, on the 14th of July, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I cannot claim that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But you have heard that, isn't you, and that's another masking technique?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I don't know until I checked the evidence. It could have been a different frequency, a different radio network, because I had a certain designation in one radio network. I had a different one in another radio network and for those who knew me I had a yet third designation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You're talking about your own secret code names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Generally speaking, generally speaking, any of the participants could operate on three radio networks and have a different name in each of the three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the notebooks that you have before you. You did go to the 2nd Corps archive department and you did tell them that you thought that was important material, and they rejected accepting it as part of the archive material. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Not the archives of the 2nd Corps, but of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. And that's the division you became a part of after the 24th merged into the 28th. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the 28th Division is part of the 2nd Corps, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It wasn't at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But it was when you tried to turn over the documents, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: It was a time when the 28th Division was about to be comprised within the 2nd Corps, but it was under the command of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The archivists may have not accepted these notebooks because they considered them unreliable. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I've already explained, they cared much more about the stamp. They cared much more about the stamp and not the content of the material.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So there could have been a lot of other documents that were offered to the 28th Division or the 2nd Corps that may have been relevant to this case that were rejected as archived material. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: The documents that were not admitted remained with me. I did not destroy anything. I kept them, and I submitted them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And these documents that you turned over in 1999, you were still a member of the Bosnian army at that time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you kept them in your personal locker at Dekici. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Not in Dekici. In the division, because I was staying at the command of the division after the combat operations ended in Dekici. That is to say at the time of the fall of Srebrenica and several days after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So you took these documents with you in your personal locker wherever you went then. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No. No. The documents were in the centre until the last day, until it was completed. When it was completed, it was then handed over to me and then it was in my custody and I kept it. It was also -- my work post was also there, so that I didn't go anywhere from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But you had taken these documents out and showed them to other people and taken them out of your locker before they were turned over to the OTP, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: Just during the attempt to get them accepted into the archive. I tried to have them placed in the archive, and when that did not succeed, I returned them to the safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you. You are familiar with an incident that happened on July 17th, 1995, in which five young Muslim boys were released on the front and the engineering department from Zvornik had to come demine the area. You're familiar with that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid I didn't understand. Will you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: On the 17th of July, 1995, five young Muslim boys were found on the VRS side, and the engineering department was sent to the front to demine the area and they sent them back to you. And I believe that your army or your communications centre sent a thank you note to the engineering department or the Zvornik Brigade -- a thank you message.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-119
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, at this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I was able to find a receipt in B/C/S to indicate when the OTP received that information. I shared it with counsel at the break, and I can tell you it was June 18th, 1999. And I would offer the photocopies of the materials of P121 and 122 into evidence along with the pseudonym sheet, P676.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We object to the introduction of the tactical intercept notebook as unreliable. These little pieces of paper were marked down sometime during the middle of heavy traffic, combat radio wave time. And then they were written down much later. Some of the intercepts were not even written down, they were just sent directly to his superiors. I don't believe that his testimony today has proven the authenticity or reliability of P121, which is the notebook. These -- he already testified that they could not take down exactly what was being said on the intercepts, that it was impossible, and some of the intercepts were not recorded. So I don't believe that there is any consistency in the reliability of what's written in the intercept notebook, so much so that the Bosnian army wouldn't accept them as evidence in their archives. P122, we have the same arguments on that. We have no problems with P16.1 or P676.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think the document P676 with the witness's pseudonym was admitted under seal. As for the other two documents, P121 and 122, this Trial Chamber has to go over the transcript of testimony of this witness to see whether we should admit it or not. We will render our decision maybe together with other the intercepts. Could I confirm that this is the last intercept witness on your side, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes it is, Mr. President -- well, we hope it is. And I don't know if you want me to make any argument responding to Ms. Sinatra. There is some brief things which you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you like, you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'll just say briefly, because I'm sure the Court is aware of this, and if we could go into private session just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your testimony. When the usher pulls down the blinds, she will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, we do have another witness or we could put him on tomorrow. In discussions with Mr. Karnavas, this witness shouldn't take too long, so we're at -- the person's outside. Mr. Waespi will handle him, and as you know the Prosecution will not be taking very long on direct. So we're fine either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we should proceed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I have just a housekeeping matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was brought to my attention that earlier when I was referring to the previous witness, not the one we just heard, as 119, actually he was 119 and I should have been referring to P135. That's what I'm told by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. President, is a witness without protective measures and he's a witness who has been ruled by Your Honours to be called for cross-examination. We have filed an application for 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good evening, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I only have a few questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you please state for the record your full name.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: My name is Radenko Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when were you born?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of April, 1965.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where are you currently living?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember that we met yesterday and I advised you of certain rights you had, for instance, to remain silent so you need not to talk to us and to have a lawyer present. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you waived these rights and said that it was fine that we talked about your evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also told us that you would be willing today to come to the courtroom and answer questions by the parties and the Judges. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you are ready to proceed today without a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you recall being interviewed by investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor in Banja Luka on the 30th of October of 2002?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And yesterday in my office have you seen and, indeed, could you read a copy of the transcript of that interview?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was that in a language you understood?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were you given the opportunity to change anything you wanted if it wasn't correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you eventually sign a declaration, a witness statement, in the presence of a court official to say that, and I quote, "the transcript was done to the best of your knowledge and recollection." Is that what you signed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could play one of the proposed exhibits, and this is a brief clip which is part, Your Honours, of the Sarajevo -- of the Srebrenica trial video which has been introduced via Jean Rene Ruez. And that would be a videoclip named P93, P93. And if it could be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And please, Mr. Zaric, watch it, and I will ask a few questions after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, witness, looking at this videoclip we are seeing right now, do you recognise anybody on this clip?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: I recognise myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just a few seconds before, do you recognise some -- did you recognise somebody else? And perhaps if we are able to go back a few seconds and start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now do you recognise somebody else on this video still?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: There were other members of the Army of Republika Srpska who were standing there on guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember which brigade they were from?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: The people who were there were members of the Bratunac Brigade, the people that are seen in the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you just told us that you recognised yourself on the video still, the previous one. Now looking at this video still, do you recognise the person who is left from you, and I believe you are the person holding a Kalashnikov in your arm. Do you recognise the person to the left of you?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the woman or the person in uniform? Because there is a woman standing to my left here with children.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes -- no, I mean the person in uniform.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: He was also a member of the military police, just like me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell -- we can go into private session if you don't want the name to be made public. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: I would prefer it not to be released to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions to this witness, and we are submitting the transcript of his witness statement under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do have some cross, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when you met with the Prosecution, for how long did you meet with them?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I came here perhaps at about 2.00, and I left at about 4.00 or 4.30 p.m. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you speak with the Prosecution before, during, or after you had a chance to review your statement, the one that you had given back on 30th October, 2002?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't talk with them before, not before yesterday. I spoke with them last year when I provided the statement and then again yesterday. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But yesterday when you spoke to them, I take it you first had an opportunity to read your statement, a copy of your statement from 2002. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how much time did you spend reading your statement?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly how much time I spent reading it. Just as I said before, I came into the building at 2.00 and I left at about 4.00, 4.30. So I can't tell you exactly. I don't remember how much time I spent. I'm not wearing a watch, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then after that is when you said that everything that you said in the statement was true?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall and based on what I read back, that's what's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I guess I want to be very clear. Are you saying that this statement --

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you saying that this statement reflects what you said, or are you saying that everything that is in this statement is truthful as far as you understand the truth to be?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, which of the two? There were two choices. Choice number one is: This is what you said when you met with them back on 30th October, 2002. I take it the answer to that question is yes?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My second question is: And that everything that you told them then that you had a chance to read and reflect, you also believe that to be true as well?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then -- let me ask you, when you read the statement, you didn't find anything that seemed rather peculiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand whether the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was your answer no? For the interpreters, they didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you may need to speak just -- speak up just a little bit so they can hear you.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it from your statement, you were mobilised in 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was in September, September 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Two years later in September 1994, you joined the military police of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while you were a member of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade, you were receiving orders from Dragisa Jovanovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Mirko Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, it was your belief and understanding when you were questioned by the Prosecution that those two individuals were receiving their orders from Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you were asked, you were asked, who was your komandir, your commanding officer, at the time when Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that point in your statement, the one that you read yesterday, you said that you thought that it was Dragisa Jovanovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I asked the investigators then what they meant. Did they mean the military police or the entire Bratunac Brigade? And then they said that the question referred to the military police. And then I responded that my superiors were Dragisa Jovanovic, Mirko Jankovic, and that I didn't know who was -- were their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Correct. And then you stated -- but at one point you stated, and it's on page 5, lines 1 and 2, of the English version. And we can locate --

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can locate -- in your version it's, I believe, page 4, line 23, you state: "I think that Dragisa Jovanovic was the commander of the military police platoon and Mirko Jankovic was his deputy." Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My question to you today is: Do you still believe that that is a correct statement, that back in July 1995 during the fall of Srebrenica, Dragisa Jovanovic was the commander of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Judging by his attitude when he came to the military police and when he spent time with us, he would be the one to issue orders to Jankovic always and to us who were subordinated to them. But I cannot actually say if I know whether they were in charge or not, because I wasn't really interested in the command structure. And let me also say that I knew only after the fall of Srebrenica that perhaps Mr. Blagojevic had been appointed the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. Up until then, I didn't even know that he was supposed to be or thought to be the commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's discuss that a little bit. If you started with the military police back in September 1994 and Srebrenica fell in July 1995, how many months would you have been in the military police?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Ten months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, for ten month -- during that ten-month period I take it you had enough time to learn who your commanding officer was. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me tell you another thing. While I was on another position as a member of the Army of Republika Srpska, Mr. Blagojevic perhaps knows that also. I think he's perhaps the 12th or the 13th commander who came to this Bratunac Brigade. And you know that best because you have all the documents. You had them in front of you and you know who commanded and where and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you that the Bratunac Brigade was changing commanders with a great deal of regularity, but my question was with respect to your commanding officer, your komandir, with respect to the military police.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, is it your understanding here today that back in July 1995 the komandir, the commanding officer, of the Bratunac military police was Dragisa Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it, since we have that answer from you, that is why you didn't think it was necessary to make any changes with respect to that aspect of your statement yesterday when you spoke with the Prosecution. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it that you still firmly believe as you sit here today that Mirko Jankovic in July 1995 was the deputy commander of the Bratunac Brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What if I were to tell you that it was actually Mirko Jankovic who was the commander? Would you believe me?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I would believe you, because you had the documents in front of you. And -- which showed that he was the commander of the military police. Because to tell you the truth, we were issued orders by Jovanovic and Jankovic most often. But what they were and what their posts were, I don't know. But they were the ones who mostly issued our orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, from reading your statement, which should be fresh in your mind from yesterday, you would have noticed that when you spoke to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecution on 30th October, 30 October, 2002, you told them that Dragisa Jovanovic was in Potocari on the 12th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact you state that, you -- when you gave that statement, you were quite firm in your belief that Dragisa Jovanovic was there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were quite firm because you recollected an occasion where you had a personal contact with him. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where you required -- where you needed or requested some time off in order to attend a celebration, a family celebration. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so, when they questioned you about Mr. Dragisa Jovanovic, about being in Potocari, as you sit here today, just as you sat in Banja Luka in 2002, you vividly recall seeing Dragisa Jovanovic in Potocari on July 12th, and perhaps the 13th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, it's been eight years since then, so last year it was seven years ago. It's very difficult for a person to remember everything exactly. I'm not able to do that. As far as I recall when you go back a little bit, I said in Banja Luka also that I talked to him, asked him that he should let me go to this sending off, this celebration. And he granted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Well, what if I were to tell you that Dragisa Jovanovic was not only not your commanding officer, your komandir, but was not even in or around Potocari or the Bratunac area during that period of time and, in fact, that he was in Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to say about that, because I know that when I came to the military police in September, Dragisa and Mirko were the commander and the deputy commander. Which post he had in the Bratunac Brigade is something that I don't know. It was not something that I would know as a regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But what if I were to tell you that we have very reliable information from the Prosecution that Mr. Dragisa Jovanovic was not in Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995, because he was in Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: If this is the information that you got from the Prosecution, then why wouldn't I believe that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And assuming, assuming, that that information is correct, then you must be wrong?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It's possible that I made a mistake. Many -- it was many years ago. A person cannot remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the mistake is not that he was -- the mistake that you've made is, one, placing this individual in Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The mistake is that you had a conversation with this individual back on the -- during that period in 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so here we are with you positively, positively, identifying someone to be in Potocari on the 12th who was not there?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: I told the investigators in Banja Luka that I cannot remember everything exactly. And I am telling you now, I cannot say that that gentleman was wearing such-and-such a tee-shirt. To tell you the truth, there are cases where they said, well, he dyed his hair like that. I talked just before the events in Srebrenica. I talked with Jovanovic and -- because I was mostly down there towards the border with the then-Yugoslavia, now it's Serbia and Montenegro on the road. And at the checkpoint, and he would come there quite a lot to visit us, and I asked him perhaps a week before the events in Srebrenica, because I wanted to let him know that he couldn't count on me on that day at all because I had that family celebration. And he said, No problem, you can go then. So I said that in Banja Luka. I cannot recall all the details, but I know very well that I did ask him that and that he said if I'm not here, and I most probably won't be here, but it's okay for you to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in a statement that Mr. Jovanovic gave to the Prosecution, he indicates that he left around the 18th or 19th of June and returned sometime in August. So he must have been -- if Srebrenica fell on the 11th of July and if Mr. Jovanovic left Bratunac on the 18th or 19th of June, we're really speaking about at least three weeks before the fall of Srebrenica, the last time that you had actually seen Mr. Jovanovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: How do you mean? Do you mean before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You've just indicated that you saw -- that Mr. Jovanovic would come up and visit you where you were stationed?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you indicated that it was approximately a week or so before the fall of Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if Srebrenica fell on the 11th of July, that would mean that you had seen him sometime during the early days of July, the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, somewhere around there. Right?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if Mr. Jovanovic had left Bratunac on the 18th or 19th of June, it would have been a physical impossibility for you to have seen him in early July in Bratunac, because he could not be in two places at once, Trnovo and Bratunac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So -- in fact, you could be mistaken as to the last time you had actually seen him?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: I said that and I repeated that many times already, that a long time has -- it's been a long time since then. So I just remember everything vaguely. I cannot remember something that happened ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, sir. And so if we come to a point in the question where the answer is: I just don't remember, perhaps that should be the answer. Now, let me ask you this: When you were being questioned in Banja Luka, were there occasions, were there occasions, where you did not know the correct or the accurate answer and you just speculated or guessed, hoping that you were giving the correct information?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. On a couple of occasions when ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So when you were asked, for instance, in Banja Luka: When did you go to Potocari? And you said that it was on the 12th, between 1500 hours and 1600 hours, that's approximately 3.00 to 4.00 p.m., were you guessing or were you sure that that's when they had sent you?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: I've also said that I don't remember exactly what time it was, but it was after 12.00 or 1.00 p.m. I also said that I cannot remember exactly. It was in the afternoon, though, in that period from 3.00 to 4.00 p.m., from 1500 hours to 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then you were asked: "Who sent you?" And do you recall answering: "My commanders," in plural, and it should be komandirs plural, "Jankovic and Jovanovic sent me there." Do you recall stating that? I'm just asking you if you recall saying it. We're going to discuss it. Do you recall saying it? If you don't, that's okay, but it's on the paper here.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall reading it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it, since you did not correct the Prosecution, your vivid recollection is that your commanders, Jankovic and Jovanovic, did indeed send you there?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: When we got the order to go there, the officer on duty came to the command, and he said that those two had said that we should go to Potocari. And he told us who was to go up there and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, before we get to that, before we get to that, might this be an occasion, sir, one of those occasions where you were just trying to give some accurate or some information to the -- to the Prosecution and you just guessed? You assumed that Jankovic and Jovanovic, both of your komandirs, sent you there. Was this fact or was this something that you assumed and presumed and wanted to give the Prosecution some information, because after all you were being questioned as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: I most probably assumed that, because this was conveyed to us by the man who was at the guard post. So I assumed that Jovanovic and Jankovic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your statement you actually say -- do you recall reading in your statement that you were at home on the 12th and that a driver was sent to fetch you, to collect you and bring you back to the brigade? Do you recall stating that to the office -- to the gentleman in Banja Luka? Would you like me to give you the page?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So -- and I'll -- let me get it to you right now. It will take me a second, but you don't recall reading that yesterday? It's on page 7 in the English version. Do you recall reading that yesterday in your statement? It should be on page 6. Do you recall reading that yesterday in your statement? On the English version it's page 7, line 13. And it should be on page --

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: It's on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It could be page -- if you could look at page 7, line 12, that may -- it's in that vicinity, that whole area -- that whole page, actually, speaks about -- do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you see it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you read it yesterday. Right?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did that strike you as somewhat odd that they would send a chauffeur basically, someone to come pick you up from the house?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: I remember stating this in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was this one of the statements, sir, where perhaps you couldn't quite remember what happened, because after all it was seven years, but you wanted to give them some information. And so you just gave them this information?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: They came for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So are you stating that the military police came to you or are you stating -- is that your statement today? You need to answer on the mike.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is fact; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you as certain about this fact as you were about who your commanding officer was, Mr. Jovanovic? Are you that certain?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you're certain -- you're as certain as you were that Mr. Jovanovic was in Potocari, when in fact we now know that he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Sir, had I not been in Potocari, I would not be on that footage, and I cannot escape that. I was of course on that footage, and I cannot, of course, claim that I wasn't there. I said a while ago I have way of knowing what the military structure was in the Bratunac Brigade, nor who was in command there, because I was an ordinary soldier. I had to go when I was told to go. And you are fully aware of this. You have the entire command structure, you have had occasion to see it in front of you. I cannot say I ordered this or I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have one last question just before we break for the evening, Mr. President, with your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But earlier you stated that you assumed, you assumed, that it was Jovanovic and Jankovic that were sending you to Potocari because someone at the command post told you this. That was earlier what you said. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we conclude, all of us here, that no one was sent to your house to tell you that Jovanovic and Jankovic -- and/or Jankovic are asking you to go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC
utterances.text: No one came to my house to tell me Jankovic or Jovanovic told you that you are to go to Potocari. A man just came and told me: You have to be up there at the military police. And as you have read, on the 10th or 11th, I was at the border crossing towards the then-Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we're going to -- I have lots more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But we have to break for the evening, Your Honour. I appreciate going over five minutes and I want to thank the interpreters and everyone else for allowing us to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Witness, I'm afraid we have to continue tomorrow afternoon, so please do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it, because you are still under the oath. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will resume tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
